sections.title: Start here: the battery is a powder before it is a cell
ps: Every guide in this corpus that covers a cell maker starts at the cell. This one starts one step earlier, at the **{{cathode active material}}** — the black powder, roughly a third of a storage cell's cost, that is coated onto aluminium foil to make the positive electrode. Mitra Chem does not make cells. It wants to make this powder, in the United States, in a chemistry ({{LFP}}) that is made almost entirely in China.

That makes it the right company to learn three things from: what a cathode actually does inside a lithium-ion cell and why iron phosphate is the chemistry grid storage chose; how a cathode powder is manufactured and why 'making it' and 'making it at scale and on spec' are different problems; and why, since 1 January 2026, a US tax rule has turned the powder's country of origin into a commercial property worth paying for.
The one sentence to hold onto: **whoever makes the powder sets the cell's cost, its safety and — under the 2026 rules — its tax status; the hard part is not the chemistry but the tonnes.**

sections.title: What a cathode does, and why iron phosphate
ps: A lithium-ion cell stores energy by moving lithium ions between two host materials. On charge the ions leave the cathode and slide into the graphite anode; on discharge they return. The host structures are not consumed — the ions slip in and out of gaps in a crystal, which is what **{{intercalation}}** means, and it is why the reaction can repeat thousands of times.

The cathode decides two things the anode does not. First, **voltage**: the cell's voltage is the difference between the two hosts' electrochemical potentials, and since graphite sits near lithium metal, the cathode chemistry sets almost the whole number. Second, **most of the cost**: the anode is graphite, which is cheap; the cathode contains the lithium and, in nickel chemistries, the nickel and cobalt.

**{{LFP}}** — lithium iron phosphate, LiFePO4 — uses an **{{olivine}}** crystal structure in which the phosphate group holds oxygen with a strong covalent bond. That bond is the reason LFP does not release oxygen when it overheats the way a nickel-oxide cathode can, which is why it is the safer chemistry and why grid storage, which sits in containers next to other containers, chose it. The iron is cheap and everywhere. Cycle life is long because the crystal barely changes shape as lithium leaves and returns.

The price of that stability is voltage and density. LFP runs at about 3.2 V against roughly 3.7 V for **{{NMC}}**, and its **{{specific capacity}}** is around 150–160 mAh per gram of powder. Multiply the two and one gram of LFP powder stores about half a watt-hour; a kilowatt-hour of cells therefore needs somewhere between two and two-and-a-half kilograms of cathode powder once you allow for the electrode's binder, carbon and practical losses. Keep that ratio — it is the arithmetic that turns a plant's tonnes into a market's gigawatt-hours.

LFP also conducts electrons and lithium ions poorly on its own. The industry's fix is to make the particles very small and to wrap each one in a thin **{{carbon coating}}**, which is why an LFP plant is as much a particle-engineering business as a chemistry business.

**{{LMFP}}** — lithium manganese iron phosphate — swaps part of the iron for manganese. Manganese's reaction runs at about 4.1 V, so a cathode with a large manganese fraction stores 15–20% more energy per kilogram at LFP-like cost. The catch is that manganese is harder to keep in the crystal: it tends to dissolve into the electrolyte and it conducts even worse than iron, so LMFP is harder to synthesise and to keep alive over thousands of cycles. That is the chemistry GM asked Mitra Chem to develop in 2023.

sections.title: How LFP cathode powder is made, and what 'on spec' means
ps: The standard route starts with an **{{iron phosphate precursor}}** — ferric phosphate, made by reacting an iron salt with phosphoric acid — plus **{{lithium carbonate}}** and a carbon source such as glucose or sucrose. The three are milled together into a slurry, dried into a free-flowing powder by **{{spray drying}}**, and then heated for hours in a furnace under nitrogen so no oxygen reaches the iron — a step called **{{sintering}}**. The carbon source chars into the carbon coating; the iron, phosphate and lithium react into olivine. The product is milled, classified by size and packed.

The alternative is **{{hydrothermal synthesis}}**: the reaction runs in hot pressurised water, which gives finer control of particle shape at the cost of throughput and waste water. Mitra Chem's own case study describes a third choice, a **{{precursor-free synthesis}}** that skips the separate iron phosphate step and, the company says, cuts raw-material cost by up to a fifth. Its Sun Chemical partnership is the opposite bet — making the precursor domestically and co-locating it with the LFP line — and the two hedges sit side by side in the record.

What does 'on spec' mean for a powder? Three numbers dominate. **{{specific capacity}}** in mAh/g tells you how much lithium the powder gives up and takes back. **{{press density}}** — grams per cubic centimetre after the coated electrode is rolled — tells you how much of that powder fits into a given volume, and it directly sets the cell's watt-hours per litre; it is the number Mitra Chem's Sun Chemical release singles out ('high press density LFP'). **{{D50}}**, the median particle size, with the spread around it, tells you whether the powder will coat evenly and conduct well. Behind those sit impurity limits measured in parts per million, moisture, surface area and the thickness of the carbon coat.

Two more facts explain why a cathode company can be four years old and still have no customer. A cell maker does not buy on a datasheet: it builds cells with the sample powder and cycles them for months — the **{{cell qualification}}** step — before it will sign, and it repeats that for every plant and every material change. And the numbers move with scale: a powder that hits spec at a kilogram a day in a lab reactor can miss it at a tonne a day in a production kiln, because heat, mixing and drying do not scale linearly. That is the gap Mitra Chem's whole 'lab-to-production' pitch is aimed at, and it is a real gap.

Read the company's claims with this in mind. 'From 1 kg/day to 1,000 kg/day in two years' describes process transfer, not a plant. 'Roughly 20× lower cost than industry incumbents' has no denominator and no product price attached. Neither claim is false on its face; both are unverifiable, and a buyer would treat them as an invitation to test, not as a result.

sections.title: Why the supply is Chinese, and what changed on 1 January 2026
ps: China makes almost all of the world's LFP cathode powder, and it does so at a price no Western entrant has yet matched. The reasons are ordinary industrial ones: the phosphate and lithium-carbonate chemical industries are there, the cell makers who buy the powder are there, the plants were built at scale a decade ago, and a price war in 2023–2025 pushed LFP powder to a level at which several Chinese producers themselves lost money. A new plant elsewhere starts at higher cost and, until it ships, at zero volume.

Western policy answered with two instruments. The first is a payment: **{{45X}}**, the advanced manufacturing production credit, pays a US cathode producer 10% of its production cost. The second is a rule that turns provenance into a requirement. From 1 January 2026, a storage project that wants the investment tax credit must show that no more than a set share of its equipment cost came from a **{{prohibited foreign entity}}** — the **{{material assistance cost ratio}}**, starting at 55% non-PFE content for storage and rising to 75% after 2029, with a parallel and steeper ladder for the 45X manufacturer itself.

Do the arithmetic and the cathode falls out as the pinch point. Cells are about half of a storage system's equipment cost, and the cathode is the largest single cost inside the cell. A project can buy a US-assembled container with US steel, US inverters and US software, and still fail the ratio if the cell inside carries a Chinese cathode. That is why the State of Michigan now describes Mitra Chem's plant in the language of provenance — 'Foreign Entity of Concern-free' and compliant with defense supply-chain rules — rather than in the language of chemistry.

Provenance is a commercial property with a price, and the price is set by how few alternatives exist. In November 2025 ICL, the Israeli chemicals group, cancelled the only other DOE-funded US LFP cathode plant after its grant was withdrawn, citing weak EV demand. That left one project in the US pipeline. The same fact cuts both ways: an entrant with no competitor has a market to itself, and a market that could not support a well-capitalised incumbent's plant may not support a start-up's either.

sections.title: How a federal grant becomes a plant — selected, obligated, outlaid
sections.intro: The words matter. 'Selected' is a press release; 'obligated' is a signed agreement; 'outlaid' is money that left the Treasury. Mitra Chem's award passed through all three states, and the amounts at each are different numbers.

items.label: Selection announced

items.label: Obligation

items.label: Second modification ($0), retitled IIJA

sections.note: A grant obligation is a ceiling, not a cheque: money is drawn against invoices as milestones are met, and a recorded period of performance that has ended without an extension is a question to ask, not a conclusion to draw.

sections.title: Reading a private company from the outside
ps: A private US company owes the public almost nothing. What it does owe, when it sells shares to investors under the most common exemption, is a **{{Form D}}** — a short notice to the SEC that states the size of the offering, how much has been sold so far, how many investors bought, the date of the first sale, and the names of the directors and officers. It does not state the price per share, the valuation, revenue or profit. Mitra Chem has filed four: two in 2021 totalling $20 million, one in 2023 showing $27.05 million sold of a $60 million round, and one in June 2025 showing $15.6 million sold of a $50 million round.

Three habits make that record useful. First, add up what was actually sold, not what was targeted: $62.6 million across four filings, against a company that has said 'nearly $80 million' and a podcast host who said '$100 million'. Second, notice what is absent: no filing after June 2025 means no public evidence the 2025 round closed. Third, use a counterparty's disclosure to triangulate — L&F, a listed Korean company, said it paid about $10 million for 3.3%, which implies a post-money value near $300 million; that is arithmetic on someone else's number, and the guide labels it as such.

Then read the company's own channels for cadence. Mitra Chem issued nineteen press releases between November 2021 and September 2024 and none since. Every material fact of 2025 and 2026 — the round, the Korean investor, the grant's survival, the doubling of state support, the slip to 2027 — reached the public through the SEC, the State of Michigan, L&F or a reporter the company did not answer. Silence is not evidence of failure; it is evidence that the next fact will come from someone else, and that the status must be re-checked rather than assumed.

Finally, keep a list of the claims that travel further than their source. 'Joint venture' appears in Korean headlines and in no filing. 'Confirmed as retained' is the State of Michigan's phrase; no DOE document names the project. '$242 million raised' on an aggregator includes the government grant. 'Valued at $250 million' is a podcast introduction. None of these is a lie, and none should be repeated as a fact.

cards.q: What is cathode active material, and roughly what share of a storage cell's cost is it?
cards.a: The powder coated onto the positive electrode's aluminium foil — the host that lithium ions leave on charge and return to on discharge. It is the single largest cost inside a lithium-ion cell, roughly a third, because it carries the lithium and, in nickel chemistries, the nickel and cobalt.

cards.q: Why is LFP the safer cathode, and what does it give up for that?
cards.a: The phosphate group in LFP's olivine crystal holds oxygen with a strong covalent bond, so an overheated LFP cell does not release oxygen the way a nickel-oxide cathode can. The price is a lower voltage (about 3.2 V against 3.7 V for NMC) and lower energy density.

cards.q: Why does LFP powder need a carbon coating and nano-sized particles?
cards.a: Because the olivine structure conducts both electrons and lithium ions poorly. Small particles shorten the path the ions must travel and a thin carbon shell around each particle carries the electrons — which makes an LFP plant a particle-engineering business as much as a chemistry business.

cards.q: What does LMFP change, and what is the cost of the change?
cards.a: It replaces part of the iron with manganese, whose reaction runs at about 4.1 V, raising energy per kilogram by 15–20% at similar material cost. Manganese is harder to keep in the crystal — it dissolves into the electrolyte and conducts worse — so LMFP is harder to make and to keep alive over thousands of cycles.

cards.q: Name the three numbers that define whether a cathode powder is 'on spec'.
cards.a: Specific capacity (mAh per gram — how much lithium it gives up and takes back), press density (grams per cubic centimetre in the rolled electrode — how much powder fits in a volume, which sets Wh per litre) and D50 particle size with its distribution (whether it coats evenly and conducts well).

cards.q: Walk through the standard route for making LFP powder.
cards.a: Mill an iron phosphate precursor, lithium carbonate and a carbon source into a slurry; spray-dry it into a free-flowing powder; sinter it for hours under nitrogen so the iron is not oxidised while the carbon source chars into the coating and the olivine forms; then mill, classify and pack.

cards.q: Why can a cathode powder hit spec in the lab and miss it in the plant?
cards.a: Heat transfer, mixing and drying do not scale linearly: a kiln handling a tonne a day has different temperature gradients and residence times from a lab reactor handling a kilogram, so particle size, coating thickness and impurities drift. Process transfer, not chemistry, is the usual failure point.

cards.q: Why does a cathode company with good samples still have no customers after years?
cards.a: Cell makers qualify a material by building cells with it and cycling them for months, then repeat the exercise for every new plant or process change. Qualification lags the powder by a year or more, and it cannot finish for a plant that does not yet exist.

cards.q: Roughly how many gigawatt-hours of LFP cells does 15,000 tonnes of cathode make, and why does that matter?
cards.a: At two to two-and-a-half kilograms of cathode per kilowatt-hour, about 6–7 GWh a year — a fraction of one large cell plant. It shows that a plant billed as 'nearly doubling US LFP capacity' is small against the cell makers it would supply.

cards.q: What is the material assistance cost ratio and why does it make the cathode the pinch point?
cards.a: The share of a project's or manufacturer's relevant cost that must come from non-prohibited-foreign-entity sources to keep the tax credit — 55% for storage in 2026 rising to 75% after 2029. Cells are about half of a storage system's equipment cost and the cathode is the largest cost inside the cell, so a Chinese cathode can fail the ratio for an otherwise domestic system.

cards.q: What does 45X pay a domestic cathode producer?
cards.a: A production credit equal to 10% of the cost of producing electrode active materials, transferable to other taxpayers, subject from 2026 to the prohibited-foreign-entity tests. It pays per unit produced, so it is worth nothing until the plant runs.

cards.q: Distinguish 'selected', 'obligated' and 'outlaid' for a federal grant.
cards.a: Selected is an announcement that creates no obligation; obligated is a signed grant agreement that commits the money against milestones and is hard to cancel; outlaid is money actually paid out against invoices. Mitra Chem's award was selected in September 2024, obligated in December 2024 for $100M, and had outlaid about $2.25M by July 2026.

cards.q: What does an SEC Form D tell you about a private company, and what does it not?
cards.a: It states the offering size, the amount sold so far, the number of investors, the date of first sale and the directors and officers. It does not state price per share, valuation, revenue or profit — and the absence of a later filing means there is no public evidence the round closed.

cards.q: How would you estimate a private company's valuation from a strategic investor's disclosure?
cards.a: Divide the amount paid by the stake bought — $10 million for 3.3% implies a post-money value near $300 million — and label the result as arithmetic on a third party's figure, not a disclosed valuation.

items.q: A storage developer buys a container assembled in Texas with US steel, US inverters and US software, but the cells inside use Chinese LFP cathode. Under the 2026 rules, what is the most likely consequence for its tax credit?
c: None — the container was assembled in the US
It may fail the material assistance cost ratio, because cells are about half of equipment cost and the cathode is the largest cost inside the cell
It loses the credit entirely regardless of other content
It qualifies for 45X instead
items.why: The ratio is measured on cost, and the cell — with its cathode — is the largest block of it. Everything else in the container can be domestic and the project can still miss the 55% threshold. 45X is a manufacturer's credit, not a project's.

items.q: A company says its LFP powder scales 'from 1 kg/day to 1,000 kg/day in two years at roughly 20× lower cost than incumbents'. What is the best reading?
c: A verified product specification
A claim about process transfer with no product price or denominator — an invitation to test, not a result
Proof the plant will be profitable
A statement about energy density
items.why: Scale-up ratios describe the path from lab to production, which is real and hard, but neither claim carries a number a buyer could check. The correct response is a qualification programme.

items.q: Why does LFP need a carbon coating?
c: To make it safer in a fire
To raise its voltage
Because the olivine structure conducts electrons poorly and the coating carries current between particles
To stop lithium from intercalating
items.why: LFP's stability comes from the phosphate bond, but the same structure is a poor electronic conductor. Nano-sizing shortens the ion path and the carbon shell provides the electron path.

items.q: A federal award shows $100 million obligated and $2.25 million outlaid eighteen months later. Which statement is correct?
c: The grant has been cancelled
The company has received $100 million
The agreement is signed and money is being drawn against early milestones; construction spending has not started
The award was never more than a selection
items.why: Obligation is the signed ceiling; outlays track actual invoices. Two per cent drawn is consistent with engineering and permitting, not with building. It also explains why the award survived reviews — there was little to claw back.

items.q: Which of these is the strongest public evidence that Mitra Chem's 2025 round closed?
c: TechCrunch's report of a $50 million target
L&F's disclosure of a $10 million investment
A Form D or Form D/A filed after 9 June 2025 showing the amount sold
The State of Michigan's 2026 release
items.why: Only a later SEC notice would show the sold amount rising toward the target. TechCrunch reported the target, L&F reported its own slice, and Michigan's release does not mention the round. None exists on the public record as of September 2026.

items.q: Why might a competitor's exit (ICL, November 2025) be bad news as well as good for the remaining entrant?
c: It is only good news — the market is now uncontested
ICL left citing weak demand and withdrawn funding, and those conditions apply to the remaining entrant's market and financing too
ICL will now supply from Israel instead
It means DOE will redirect ICL's grant to the survivor
items.why: An incumbent chemicals group with its own balance sheet judged the plant unbuildable without the grant and against the demand it saw. The survivor inherits the position and the same question about demand, and DOE grants are not reassigned.

glossary.d: The extra price a buyer will pay for a material because of where and by whom it was made rather than what it is — in US battery storage since 2026, the value of cathode that keeps a project under the material-assistance cost ratio. A market term used in this guide, not a regulatory one.
